name: Nominalism
statement: Only particular, concrete things exist; there are no universals or abstract objects.
meaning: Nominalism is, broadly, the metaphysical position that denies the existence of certain kinds of abstract or universal entities, holding that reality is made up only of particulars. There are two main and separable senses of the term. In one sense, nominalism is the denial of universals: the view that there are no universals, only particulars, offered as an answer to the problem of universals and opposed to realism about universals. In the other sense, nominalism is the denial of abstract objects: the view that there are no abstract objects, such as numbers, sets, or propositions, only concrete objects, opposed to Platonism about the abstract. The two theses are related but come apart, and a view can be nominalist in one sense without being nominalist in the other. Nominalism about universals must explain why distinct things can share a feature, why two things are both red, without positing a shared universal, and it does so in various ways, including predicate, concept, resemblance, class, and mereological nominalism, and the austere or ostrich nominalism associated with W. V. O. Quine, which treats predication as primitive. Nominalism about mathematics denies that numbers exist as abstract objects and must answer the Quine-Putnam indispensability argument, as in Hartry Field's program. Nominalism has deep historical roots in the medieval universals debate, in Roscelin, Abelard, and William of Ockham, and it is motivated by ontological parsimony and Ockham's razor.
mechanism: Nominalism proceeds by refusing to admit universals or abstract objects into its ontology and then finding other resources to do the work such entities were meant to do. On universals, the nominalist accepts that things can be similar, that two apples are both red, but denies that there is a further entity, redness, that they share. Different nominalisms then explain shared nature differently. Predicate nominalism says a thing is red simply because the predicate red is true of it, taking predication as basic. Concept nominalism grounds it in falling under a concept. Resemblance nominalism, developed by Gonzalo Rodriguez-Pereyra, holds that a thing is red in virtue of resembling other red particulars, so that resemblance classes replace universals. Class nominalism identifies a property with the class of things that have it. Austere or ostrich nominalism, associated with Quine and so named pejoratively by Armstrong, denies that the one-over-many demands any ontological explanation at all: that many things are red is just many particular facts, and no shared entity or analysis is owed. On abstract objects, nominalism about mathematics denies that numbers and sets exist as mind-independent abstracta, which runs up against the Quine-Putnam indispensability argument, that since our best scientific theories quantify over numbers, we ought to believe they exist. Nominalists respond either by reconstruing mathematics without abstracta, as in Hartry Field's attempt to do science without numbers, treating mathematics as a useful fiction, or by accepting the indispensability of mathematical talk while denying that it commits us to abstract objects. Throughout, the driving motivation is parsimony: fewer kinds of entity make for a leaner, more defensible ontology.

examples.text: Nominalism denies universals, holding only particulars exist, or denies abstract objects, holding only concrete things exist.
A thing is red in virtue of resembling other red particulars, so resemblance classes replace shared universals.
Quine's austere nominalism denies the one-over-many needs any ontological explanation, taking predication as primitive.

whyItMatters: Nominalism is one of the two great options in the problem of universals and a central position in debates over abstract objects, and it has shaped metaphysics from the medieval schools to contemporary philosophy of mathematics. Its appeal is the appeal of ontological economy: by admitting only particulars, or only concrete objects, nominalism honors Ockham's razor and the empiricist suspicion of entities that cannot be perceived, offering a leaner picture of reality than realism or Platonism. Engaging with nominalism sharpens the deepest questions in ontology, about what there is, about how language and predication relate to the world, about the nature of resemblance and natural kinds, and about the status of mathematics, one of our most successful and seemingly indispensable forms of knowledge. The medieval nominalists, Roscelin with his puffs of voice, Abelard, and above all Ockham, made nominalism a permanent option, and modern nominalists such as Quine and Field have pressed it in logic and the philosophy of science, giving rise to the indispensability debate and to fictionalist programs. Even realists must define themselves against the nominalist challenge to justify their richer ontology.

working.text: admit into the ontology only particulars, or only concrete objects, denying universals or abstracta.
account for shared features through predicates, resemblance, or classes of particulars, not a shared universal.
for mathematics, either reconstrue it without numbers or deny that its usefulness commits one to abstract objects.

limits: Nominalism faces serious objections in both its main forms. Against nominalism about universals, realists argue that it cannot adequately explain objective resemblance and predication without covertly reintroducing a universal or leaving the one-over-many unanswered: predicate nominalism seems to reverse the order of explanation, making things red because red is true of them rather than the reverse, and resemblance nominalism confronts the companionship problem, where co-extensive properties cannot be distinguished, and the imperfect-community problem, both raised by Nelson Goodman, that mere pairwise resemblance need not pick out a genuine shared property. Austere nominalism is charged with dodging the problem rather than solving it. Against nominalism about abstract objects, the Quine-Putnam indispensability argument presses that we cannot do our best science without quantifying over numbers, so we ought to believe in them, and nominalist reconstruals such as Field's are technically demanding and disputed. Ostrich is Armstrong's pejorative for Quine's austere nominalism, the Quine-Putnam joint label is standard though Quine's 1948 formulation is foundational, and Field's Science Without Numbers dates to 1980.
misreadings: Nominalism is not the denial that things resemble one another or share features in some loose sense; it denies that a shared universal, or an abstract object, exists to ground this. Its two senses are distinct, since denying universals is not the same as denying abstract objects, and one can hold either without the other. And nominalism about mathematics is not the claim that mathematics is false or useless, since fictionalists grant its usefulness while denying its objects exist, so treating nominalism as denying all similarity, as a single thesis, or as rejecting mathematics itself, misreads the position.
origin: The metaphysical position, rooted in the medieval universals debate and developed by Ockham, Quine, and Field, that denies universals, or abstract objects, holding that reality consists only of particulars or only of concrete things.
